title: Connecting Landscapes: A Practical Tutorial for Ecological Connectivity Modelling

title: 2  Introduction
text:
As introduced in Section 1.4b, there are numerous forms of connectivity models from the purely functional models using GPS tracking data of animals to structural metrics that quantify the spatial arrangement of different land cover patches. Access to these different models is spread across several different software packages with varying levels of interactive interface. Most exist as package libraries in R and/or Python. Others such as least-cost path models and the Linkage Mapper tool suite are available on interactive GIS platforms like ArcGIS or QGIS.
Some of the most commonly used models today are those that use a cost or resistance surface to model potential movement pathways either from point A to point B or continuously across the full landscape. Models such as

least-cost path
randomized shortest paths
resistant kernels
Circuitscape and Omniscape

use a resistance raster. While most, including least-cost path and Cricuitscape, require the input of at least one start and end node (points or polygons), Omniscape computes movement from every direction. These models have grown in popularity, in part, because of their relative accessibility to modelers and practitioners for management decisions and the spatial data that are created which can communicate connectivity concepts and concerns to stakeholders.

title: 3  Exercise Background
text:
3.1 Data Inputs
We can download the data from our Github repository. Our dataset will include polygons and points that represent the protected areas in our study area and a resistance raster for large predators. The name of the file that we will be using is below in italics.

title: 3  Exercise Background
text:
Polygon of protected areas: “PA_balkan_subset.shp”

This is a subset of protected areas clipped for the study region from the World Database of Protected Area (WDPA) and edited to reduce overlapping polygons.

Protected area centroid points: “PA_balkan_subset_pts2.shp”

Centroids are the centre point of each of the protected area polygons. The centroids are then further divded between places where an animal starts moving from to multiple different end points.

Starting point–“start_pts_mne.shp”
End points–“end_pts_balkans.shp”


Resistance raster: “balkan_predenergy_resist.tif”

The resistance surface was generated for large predators using a combination of species distribution models and an energy expenditure model. The SDM quantifies habitat suitability on a 0.0-1.0 scale with 1.0 being the highest/best habitat suitability and 0.0 being the lowest.
We then invert the SDM values so that areas with the highest habitat suitability have the lowest resistance to movement. The energy expenditure model quantifies how topography impacts the potential caloric energy used by a large mammal as it moves across the landscape. Very rugged or steep slopes therefore have much higher energy values than flatlands.
The resistance data is at a resolution of 1 km x 1km cells. This can be rather coarse and can slightly bias the corridor paths which we will discuss some outside.

title: 4  Least-Cost Path in QGIS
text:
4.1 QGIS Protocol
We will produce least-cost paths (LCP) for large predators dispersing from one national park in Montenegro to a more than 20 other protected areas within the region. We provide an introduction to the protocol of operations in QGIS then a video walking you through the full short exercise. These are real scientific data and the LCPs we produce could provide valuable insight for connectivity conservation in the central Balkans.

title: 5  Least-cost Path in Program R
text:
5.1 Connectivity Analysis in Program R
Having looked at the LCP analysis in QGIS we can now explore connectivity modelling in R which will allow for more options and flexibility. We will rely upon the ‘terra’ package for raster processing and some vector data handling. Connectivity modelling will be handled by the ‘leastcostpath’ package for least-cost path analysis
crumbs: 5  Least-cost Path in Program R

title: 5  Least-cost Path in Program R
text:
5.2 Least-cost Path Analysis
We will use the same data that we used in QGIS, but in R we can choose which pairs we want to make a connection rather than just one start point and multiple end points. First, lets load the necessary packages and data and perform some pre-processing steps. The ‘leastcostpath’ package is relatively new and is an upgrade to the ‘gdistance’ package (which requires the use of the outdated ‘raster’ package).

library(leastcostpath)
library(terra)
library(sf)

pts = st_read("./data/PA_balkan_subset_pts2.shp")
polygons = st_read("./data/PA_balkan_subset.shp")
resist = rast("./data/balkan_predenergy_resist.tif")

Let’s take a quick look at the data in the central Balkans.


plot(resist,
     main = "Resistance Surface")

plot(st_geometry(polygons),
     add = TRUE,
     border = "coral3",
     col = "coral")

plot(st_geometry(pts),
     add = TRUE,
     pch = 16,
     col = "red",
     cex = 0.7)








Let’s choose an origin for the LCP analysis in which to connect to several other nearby protected areas.

origin = pts[107, ]
dest = c(3, 4, 23, 34, 35, 36, 43, 46, 50, 52, 54, 55, 56, 62, 74, 84, 95)
destinations = pts[dest, ]
plot(resist)
plot(destinations, add = TRUE, pch = 16, col = "red")








After we have defined the origin and destinations we need to then calculate a conductance matrix for the calculation of the least-cost paths. The create_cs() function translates the resistance raster into a form that the create_lcp() can use to calculate all the individual least-cost paths. Finally we can plug in this matrix and our different points layers and calculate the paths.

cs_matrix = create_cs(resist, neighbours = 16, max_slope = NULL, exaggeration = FALSE)

paths = create_lcp(cs_matrix, origin, destinations, cost_distance = TRUE)

plot(resist)

plot(st_geometry(polygons),
     add = TRUE,
     border = "coral3",
     col = "coral")


plot(st_geometry(paths),
     add = TRUE,
     col = "blue",
     lwd = 2)

plot(st_geometry(origin),
     add = TRUE,
     pch = 16,
     col = "red",
     cex = 1.5)

plot(st_geometry(destinations),
     add = TRUE,
     pch = 16,
     col = "black")








An additional visual that could be helpful for conservation managers is a density raster of the least-cost paths. The leastcostpath package luckily has a function that does just that!

density = create_lcp_density(resist, paths)

plot(density)

plot(st_geometry(pts),
    add = TRUE,
    border = "coral3",
    col = "coral")








The output is rather faint since the vast amount of the landscape does not have overlapping LCPs. However, some overlapping lines are visible surrounding the first ~50 kilometers from the protected area.

title: 6  Circuitscape Exercise in R
text:
6.1 Circuitscape Analysis [Under construction!]
Now that we have seen how to perform least-cost path exercises in QGIS and R, we will move on to operating and understanding circuit-theory models. Where least-cost path models create a single path between a pair of points (e.g. between two protected areas), circuit-theory models, such as Circuitscape, create many potential paths that could be create via “random-walking” simulations. This is likely a more realistic representation of how wildlife interact and move through their environment.
The R library ‘circuitscaper’ provides an R-native interface to the most recent versions of Circuitscape and Omniscape. These two programs are written in the Julia code language therefore you will first need to download Julia using the ‘circuitscaper’ function cs_install_julia() or if you prefer download Julia directly from the code language’s official website. We will get started just like in the least-cost path analysis by loading in and sub-setting our data.
#As with all R packages, you will initially need to use install.packages("circuitscaper") in order to install the package on your computer. 

library(circuitscaper)
library(terra)
library(sf)

resist = rast("./data/balkan_predenergy_resist.tif")

pts = st_read("./data/PA_balkan_subset_pts2.shp")
#> Reading layer `PA_balkan_subset_pts2' from data source 
#>   `C:\Users\no67wuwu\Documents\naturaConnect\connectivity_tutorial\Connectivity_LearningPlatform\docs\data\PA_balkan_subset_pts2.shp' 
#>   using driver `ESRI Shapefile'
#> Simple feature collection with 108 features and 4 fields
#> Geometry type: POINT
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 4903768 ymin: 2070317 xmax: 5320284 ymax: 2433989
#> Projected CRS: ETRS89-extended / LAEA Europe


#Subset the data for the same nodes as the least-cost path analysis
origin = pts[107, ]
destinations = pts[c(3, 4, 23, 34, 35, 36, 43, 46, 50, 52, 54, 55, 56, 62, 74, 84, 95), ]

focal_pts = rbind(origin, destinations)

plot(resist)

plot(st_geometry(focal_pts),
     add = TRUE, 
     pch = 16,
     col = "red")
Running this next function will download Julia and Circuitscape to your computer, therefore, it may not be necessary if you have already downloaded these programs onto your computer.
# This will download Julia and the latest versions of Circuitscape.jl and Omniscape.jl
cs_install_julia(version = "latest")
Later, if you are having issues with R finding Julia or Circuitscape, it may be necessary to use the cs_setup() function to explicitly control the file path of Julia on your computer.
Similar to the least-cost path exercise in R, we will subset the points data to one origin point and multiple destination connections.
#Subset the data for the same nodes as the least-cost path analysis
origin = pts[107, ]
destinations = pts[c(3, 4, 23, 34, 35, 36, 43, 46, 50, 52, 54, 55, 56, 62, 74, 84, 95), ]

focal_pts = rbind(origin, destinations)

plot(resist)

plot(st_geometry(focal_pts),
     add = TRUE, 
     pch = 16,
     col = "red")

title: 6  Circuitscape Exercise in R
text:
6.1.1 Running Circuitscape
We will convert the points into coordinates since ‘circuitscaper’ accepts a two-column matrix or data frame of x/y coordinates and internally converts those locations to focal node raster cells. Then we run Circuitscape from our one origin point (protected area) to all our destination points. It is useful to first run ?cs_one_to_all() to see the defaults of all the parameters running in the Circuitscape call.

coords = st_coordinates(focal_pts)

coords
#>             X       Y
#>  [1,] 5113397 2224200
#>  [2,] 5209165 2127722
#>  [3,] 5023029 2287252
#>  [4,] 5193241 2147887
#>  [5,] 5039493 2280885
#>  [6,] 5099280 2334207
#>  [7,] 5169310 2130558
#>  [8,] 5017686 2210870
#>  [9,] 5222627 2163670
#> [10,] 5047381 2292216
#> [11,] 5253998 2150047
#> [12,] 5125907 2254140
#> [13,] 5103056 2212571
#> [14,] 5056657 2269728
#> [15,] 5038216 2249313
#> [16,] 5121360 2201187
#> [17,] 5216569 2178440
#> [18,] 5153654 2235327

#Currently the analysis is only saving the cumulative of all the pair-to-pair current density calculations. 
#If you want to save each pair's directional connectivity calculation change cumulative_only = FALSE .

cs_result = cs_one_to_all(
  resistance = resist,
  locations = coords,
  resistance_is = "resistances",
  cumulative_only = TRUE
)

#Check out the cumulative current results and then plot the data
cs_result$cumulative_current
#> class       : SpatRaster 
#> size        : 377, 465, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 1000, 1000  (x, y)
#> extent      : 4868000, 5333000, 2060439, 2437439  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : ETRS89 Lambert Azimutal Equal Area 
#> source(s)   : memory
#> varname     : cs_output_cum_curmap 
#> name        : cumulative_current 
#> min value   :           0.000000 
#> max value   :           2.418532

plot(
  cs_result$cumulative_current,
  main = "Cumulative Current Density"
)

plot(
  st_geometry(focal_pts),
  add = TRUE,
  pch = 16,
  col = "red"
)








Higher values identify areas that are receiving more current across between and within protected areas in your network. Ecologically this can indicate the more important areas for wildlife movement or where connectivity corridors are being highly compressed and possibly under threat from being cutoff.
We can identify potential hotspots for connectivity by isolating the highest percentile values of current density.

current = cs_result$cumulative_current

vals = values(current, mat = FALSE)

vals = vals[is.finite(vals) & vals > 0]

#This will identify the top 10% value threshold
threshold_90 = quantile(
  vals,
  probs = 0.90,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

threshold_90
#>        90% 
#> 0.02753721

hotspots10 = current >= threshold_90

plot(hotspots10,
  main = "Top 10% Current-Density Hotspots"
)

plot(st_geometry(focal_pts),
  add = TRUE,
  pch = 16,
  col = "red"
)








Isolating other threshold values is rather simple. If you want to identify the top 5% or top 25% just change the threshold_90 object, respectively:
threshold_95 = quantile(vals, 0.95)
threshold_75 = quantile(vals, 0.75)
These different rasters can be overlaid in one plot to easily see transitions in the hotspot areas.
